plan.day: 9am video standup on my laptop, lunch with a client by the window, dinner date at 7

moments.title: Morning standup
assumptions: I took the laptop camera as about arm's length away and the team call as a gallery view.

notice.text: A typical viewer could pick out about a third of your dark spots, and under-eye shadows and puffiness would be noticeable.

outOfSight.text: On the call, pores and fine lines come out as none for a typical viewer, and the video itself carries nothing finer than 2.4 mm.
Most breakouts are lost in the video too, with 17 of 18 below what the camera can carry.

claim.text: Moving the camera back does not help much, since even with it 90 cm away in gallery view dark spots (about 1 in 8) would still be picked out.

moments.title: Lunch with a client by the window
assumptions: I took the window seat as bright daylight and a small table as close, about arm's length.

notice.text: At 80 cm in bright daylight a typical viewer could pick out nearly all dark spots and breakouts, and most pores and fine lines.
Under-eye shadows and puffiness would also be noticeable, which is simply how close and bright this seat is.

claim.text: If you want to soften breakouts, 75% coverage, measured in indoor light at 1.5 m, gets most of the effect but not all of it.

moments.title: Dinner date
assumptions: I took the dinner as dim evening light at home or a restaurant, across a table.

notice.text: A typical viewer could pick out most dark spots, about a third of fine lines and about 1 in 9 breakouts.
Under-eye shadows and puffiness would be noticeable.

outOfSight.text: At 1.5 m in evening light at home, only about 1 in 30 pores can be picked out by a typical viewer.

claim.text: Only if you wish, 100% coverage on dark spots, measured in indoor light at 1.5 m, gets most of the effect but not all of it.

summary.text: Across the day, pores and fine lines are out of sight on the call, and at dinner only about 1 in 30 pores can be picked out; lunch by the window is the closest, brightest moment.

assumptions: Distance: the other person sees you on a screen tile, so the moment is judged at the in-person distance your face would look the same size from (see the video call numbers).
Light: video call light. On a video call the other person's eyes are adapted to a screen of 200 to 300 cd/m2, and a face on it is about 0.35 of white.
Viewer: a typical person with 20/20 sight, looking right at the mark, with nothing else competing for their attention.
'About' numbers are for an average observer. 'At most' numbers are for even perfect eyes (a 6 dB margin on top of the average observer), so a real viewer sees the same or less.
Sizes in millimetres use your iris as the ruler (about 4% uncertainty), so they carry that uncertainty too.
Masks and contrasts come from one photo; hair, glasses, make-up, movement and a different angle will change what is seen.
Project assumption: a built-in laptop webcam is roughly 80 degrees diagonal, which on a 16:9 frame is about 46 degrees vertical.

Project assumption: about 50 cm, the near end of the 50 to 100 cm usually advised for monitor distance (OSHA computer workstations guidance). The most you can sit back and still reach the keys is taken as 90 cm.
Project assumption: they sit about 60 cm from a laptop screen, inside the 50 to 100 cm usually advised for monitor distance (OSHA computer workstations guidance).
Project assumption: on a 15-inch laptop screen (about 19 cm tall) a speaker view fills about 17 cm and a gallery tile of four to nine people about 7 cm.

Project assumption: calls send about 720 rows to a large tile (HD) and about 360 rows to a small gallery tile, as video-call services scale each person's picture to the tile it fills. The smallest detail the video carries is taken as two rows of pixels.
The whole camera frame is assumed to fill the height of the tile.
Video compression hides more than this removes, so the distance is a cautious estimate: the real picture is, if anything, softer.
Marks smaller than the video's smallest detail are counted as lost in the video, whatever the other person's eyes.

assumptions: Measured in indoor light, at 1.5 m, with a typical viewer looking right at it.
This is a virtual try-on of foundation, run once on your photo; real makeup, shade and light will differ.
Coverage is the try-on's own scale from 0 to 100, not a property of any product on a shelf.
The goal is that even perfect eyes could pick out at most 1 in 10 of them across a table; where makeup cannot reach that, the coverage shown is where most of the effect is reached.
